title: Cutchogue
summary: Cutchogue is a Southold placename connected with the modern hamlet and an older Corchaug tract. It as a post-office and farming hamlet and notes that the name originally applied to land where a Corchaug village stood on Fort Neck. Quochague is a later record form treated as a Cutchogue cross-reference. The name is interpreted as the principal place.
address_label: Cutchogue / Fort Neck, Town of Southold, NY
history_content: Several early forms of Cutchogue are preserved, including Corchauge, Cauchaug, Courchauge, Corchogge, Kachogue, and Cauchauk. Fort Neck is treated as the place of the palisaded village and Cutchogue as the principal place of the local community. A 1787 deposition refers to a fence at Little Neck in Quochague; that dated record is listed in the timeline.
translation_content:
Recorded forms include Cutchogue, Corchauge, Cauchaug, Courchauge, Corchogge, Cauchauk, Kachogue, Catsjeyick, Catsjajock, Catsjey, Catsja, Carch, and Caugh. The name is interpreted as the greatest or principal place, from a word for chief, superior, or principal plus a locative ending.

Why Place Names Matter

“The material reality of inequities and hierarchies result from the mapping process of naming and symbolically defining and enframing land.”

— Mishuana Goeman, Mark My Words: Native Women Mapping Our Nations (2013), Introduction, page 23
land_loss_content: Cutchogue preserves the name of a principal Corchaug place within a North Fork landscape now often mapped through hamlets, farms, roads, and archaeological labels. Presenting the placename beside Fort Neck context keeps the older Indigenous geography visible without reducing it to a single excavation point.
whereintheworld_content: The name is associated broadly with modern Cutchogue and with the older Fort Neck village and tract described by Tooker. Exact historic boundaries remain uncertain.
